full_content:
如果能“长命百岁”，你愿意吗？


7月28日，在上海一场聚焦长寿的发布会上，平安好医生CEO何明科抛出了这个可能会收获许多肯定答案的问题。


不过，先不要急着回答。来对比一组数据：


2025年，中国人均预期寿命已超79岁，“十五五”末有望迈入80岁区间。


另一个现实是，由亚太长寿医学学会、中国抗衰老促进会、平安好医生联合撰写的《2026高质量健康长寿白皮书》指出，健康预期寿命与预期寿命之间存在显著“剪刀差”。因为，据WHO数据，中国健康预期寿命仅为68.5岁。


所以，如果晚年生活有很长一段时间在病痛中度过，你还愿意“长命百岁”吗？这时可能会有更多否定答案了。



当下，肿瘤新药、细胞抗衰、脑机接口等前沿技术研发投入不断加码，新产品持续涌现。在科技浪潮下，以长寿为导向的前沿技术快速迭代、不断刷新大众认知。叠加卫生健康服务体系的进步，人均预期寿命持续增长。


寿命延长的另一面，是大量老年人正在与一种或多种慢病长期共存。如果说慢病在规范治疗和管理下尚可控制，那么失能失智则可能让患者本人及家庭陷入“失控”状态。据统计，截至2025年底，国内失能老年人口约3600万、失智老年人口约1700万，这不只关系着个人生命质量的降低，还涉及所有家庭成员的照护牵挂。


科技让人们活得更久，但晚年生活的健康品质并未同步跟上。


差距的根源首先在于服务体系的错位。以往，医疗健康服务在资源总量有限的前提下，更侧重于疾病治疗，前置的风险筛查、长期机能养护投入不足；分科诊疗模式割裂了健康管理应有的整体性，缺少多病共防共管的整合方案；筛查、治疗、康复、随访等环节各自独立，数据不互通、服务不连贯，患者需辗转多家机构，健康管理只能碎片化开展。


另一个更突出的短板是，业界对长寿的关注大多集中在生理层面。筛查看的是生理指标，慢病管理盯的是血糖血压等数据，抗衰做的是细胞和营养。心理、认知等同样直接影响晚年生活质量的维度，长期被忽略。生活中，许多与常见生理指标无关的症状，都被简单归结为“老了的正常现象”。


《2026高质量健康长寿白皮书》提出了延长健康寿命的迫切性，行业需要从被动治病转向主动前置预防，从健康维持升级到健康优化，以全周期身体机能维护来实现真正的健康寿命提升。



如何建立一套行之有效的新型长寿健康服务模式？


先来看一个直观的场景。


7月28日发布会现场，何明科现场登台演示了一段由“平安智享私教”指导的八段锦练习，这是平安好医生新推出的“AI+真人”模式下的数智健管服务。现场大屏幕同步联动平板电脑，自研DeepBody引擎则通过平板实时捕捉演示者全身骨骼关键点位，动作姿态、肢体开合幅度实时投射在屏幕上，AI实时矫正提示，线上真人私教同步讲解和点评，一屏之内实现智能识别纠错与专业人工指导同频进行。


 

平安好医生CEO何明科（左）现场演示数字化八段锦


用户使用时，只需通过平安好医生APP预约私教，之后，手机、平板或家用智能电视均可作为训练交互终端，获得健康评估、专项训练、效果巩固的运动健康闭环服务，且几乎不受时间与场地限制。


这是科技与传统养生的碰撞，也是平安好医生创新长寿健康服务的一个缩影。


与此同时，中国平安升级后的长寿管理服务体系也在发布会上展现出全貌。该体系依托医学、AI及前沿科技三大核心能力建立，基于两大关键理念，何明科将其称之为：“不下桌”，守住生命主场；“上绝活”，主动健康干预。前者主要通过前置筛查、安全应急、就医协助、多病共管的四道防线，实现风险的早识别、早筛查和早处置；后者则围绕行为层、躯体层、心智层打造主动健康干预方案。


 

平安长寿服务全景图


这套体系以平安好医生多年沉淀的“到线、到院、到家、到企”四到服务网络作为资源支撑。7月28日，平安好医生还同步成立长寿生态联盟，联合长寿健康所需的精准筛检、医药健康、营养健康、再生医学、数智康养等细分领域的合作伙伴，共同服务用户。


拆解这套体系及落地路径可以发现，它是对行业碎片化现状的系统性破解。


体系内，服务贯穿全方位的前置检筛到全周期多病共管，平安好医生还搭建起统一的数字底座，打通各类筛查、训练、管理设备之间的数据壁垒，让筛查结果能直接指导干预方案，运动数据能反馈到机能管理。


这一模式有助于从源头减少疾病发生，或延缓小病向失能、失智、重症演化，并在疾病发生后精准管控病程，持续维持机体健康状态。


同时，这套体系将心智养护提到与躯体治疗同等高度，补齐过往长寿服务的突出短板。


在平安健康长寿管理服务体系中，主动健康干预方案包括三个层面：行为层聚焦慢病长期管理与生活方式养成，躯体层包括代谢调节与身体机能养护，心智层关注脑健康综合干预。让长寿群体不只是“活着”，更要“活得好”。


正如《2026高质量健康长寿白皮书》提出的百岁健康评估体系及百岁健康标准指数（CHLI）那样，健康长寿理应关注生物学年龄、功能健康状态、代谢健康状态、生活方式与行为、心理认知与社交参与、数字化动态健康监测的全维度。

 

 


百岁健康评估体系六大维度及指数，图片来源：《2026高质量健康长寿白皮书》


作为长寿管理服务体系落地的形式之一，在7月28日的发布会上，平安好医生旗下11家平安健康长寿中心揭牌。中心以平安健康（检测）中心为载体，融合精准医学、营养学、中医学、睡眠医学、身心医学等多学科手段，构建全生命周期的健康管理闭环。这将成为全方位身心长寿健康的一个典型场景。


从行业层面看，平安健康长寿管理服务体系可借助长寿生态联盟，深度挖掘百岁健康这个增量市场。


联盟的准入标准和供应链要求为合作伙伴提供了明确的质量要求，降低了伙伴单独摸索服务标准的试错成本；同时，标准化输出的高质量服务，还可帮助合作机构拓客引流、提升用户转化率。


在此模式下，科技赋能延长健康生存年限，更长的健康寿命持续催生多元化康养需求，形成良性产业循环。



专业可靠的长寿健康服务，是不是大众都能享有？这必是长寿时代社会最关心的话题之一。


过去，在大众认知中，高端诊所、抗衰疗法、全周期健康管理、深度机能养护等价格昂贵，仅部分群体能够长期享受。这在一定程度上的确符合现实，如果优质长寿服务始终局限于小众圈层，那么缩小寿命与健康寿命之间的剪刀差便无从谈起。


对此，平安好医生依托与平安集团的医险协同优势，提升长寿管理服务的可及性：与平安寿险、平安产险、平安健康险、平安银行等合作，将长寿健康管理服务融入保险或金融产品中，形成前沿长寿科技、专业服务与支付的闭环。


医险协同模式下，规模化支付可降低长寿服务成本。平安好医生整合各类长寿健康产品与服务，依托大规模采购的议价优势，把零散的高价、单项服务转化为高性价比组合方案；优化长寿服务成本结构，让大众能够常态化、持续性享受健康养护。


同时，该模式还可促进大众消费认知的转变。当各项长寿健康管理成为组合式的权益保障，用户心态会从额外花钱买服务变为兑现已购服务。前者属于主动消费，每次支出都需谨慎决策，后者更像是福利消耗，使用服务顺理成章。


自古以来，长命百岁都是人民对生命的美好愿望。科技赋予人类更长的生命时限，朝着长命百岁的目标接近，却难以直接消除慢病、失能带来的低质量晚年。覆盖全生命周期、兼顾身心养护、普惠大众的体系化长寿健康服务，将是实现真正的健康长寿的必然选择。

title: Big Pharma’s drug marketing got stealthy, and you are the target [PODCAST]
summary: Subscribe to The Podcast by KevinMD. Watch on YouTube. Catch up on old episodes! The pharma rep with the free lunch is gone. What replaced it is harder to see, and aimed at you and your doctor. Martha...
full_content:
Subscribe to The Podcast by KevinMD. Watch on YouTube. Catch up on old episodes!

The pharma rep with the free lunch is gone. What replaced it is harder to see, and aimed at you and your doctor. Martha Rosenberg is an investigative reporter who has worked at two medical schools and two medical ad agencies, seeing drug marketing from the inside. This episode is based on her article “3 new pharma marketing tactics every physician should know,” published on KevinMD. Reporting from a pharma conference, Martha breaks down three tactics drug makers no longer hide. You will hear how AI apps track where a prescriber sits on the “prescription journey,” how disease mongering and TikTok influencers turn everyday worries into conditions worth medicating, and how the industry is shifting from “ask your doctor” ads to pop-up and online practices that sell straight to patients and sidestep the FDA. She also flags a Maryland bill that would force disclosure of pharma funding behind patient advocacy groups. Press play to learn how to spot the marketing dressed up as medicine, and why your skepticism is the best defense you have.

Partner with me on the KevinMD platform. With over three million monthly readers and half a million social media followers, I give you direct access to the doctors and patients who matter most. Whether you need a sponsored article, email campaign, video interview, or a spot right here on the podcast, I offer the trusted space your brand deserves to be heard. Let’s work together to tell your story.

PARTNER WITH KEVINMD → https://kevinmd.com/influencer

SUBSCRIBE TO THE PODCAST → https://www.kevinmd.com/podcast

Transcript

Kevin Pho: Hi, and welcome to the show. Subscribe at KevinMD.com/podcast. Today, we welcome back Martha Rosenberg. She’s an investigative reporter and writer. Today’s KevinMD article is “Three new pharma marketing tactics every physician should know.” Martha, welcome back to the show.

Martha Rosenberg: Thank you, Dr. Pho. I love to be on your podcast, and I’d like to talk about this recent article.

Kevin Pho: Absolutely. So why did you decide to write it in the first place? And then talk about the article itself for those who didn’t get a chance to read it yet.

Martha Rosenberg: Sure. OK. So in May there was a big conference in San Diego called Fierce Pharma Engage, and it’s unabashedly designed to connect health care providers with big pharma. There were 700 participants, 56 sponsors, and there’s no attempt to hide the agenda of engaging. So I wrote about three revelations from that conference, which was last month.

Kevin Pho: When you said that there was no hiding what their agenda was, what exactly was their agenda?

Martha Rosenberg: Well, they’re getting health care providers to sell drugs. I’ve been a reporter on these issues for a long time, and I can remember when doctors would be given tickets to playoffs or sent to Bermuda. Now there are different tactics used, but the idea is monetizing the drugs through buying sales.

It is not hidden. This conference was built for it. You’d see all these people, pardon the sirens here, you’d see all the people shaking hands and sharing agendas, and it was just very overt.

Kevin Pho: Now, from your perspective, over the years, how has direct pharma marketing to physicians changed? Because, like you said, back when I was a medical student and resident, there were all these lunches and dinners and being taken out to baseball games and stuff like that. But from what I understand, that has changed since then, right?

Martha Rosenberg: Well, it totally has, Dr. Pho. I might add here, for anybody watching this, that I’ve worked at two medical schools, studied at a medical school, and worked at two top medical ad agencies, so my orientation is drug marketing. I see it from both sides.

I can remember when what we used to call detail men, men and women, would come in to see the doctor with their tote bags that would mention the drug they wanted to sell. And they’d have their own room, with a water cooler and swivel chairs, and that was too overt. Now the partnerships are really different, as we see in this conference.

There’s really no attempt to hide affiliations anymore, which is one of the things I discovered at the conference: the very strong agenda of drug makers to directly market. We’ve heard about telehealth. We’ve heard about direct-to-patient advertising, but it’s really not hidden.

The plan of drug makers is to really bypass the doctors and just go direct. They want not only to engage and sell, but also to ship the drugs to the patients. So you see a lot of this online now: Talk to a doctor directly. That’s a move to hijack what used to be a system of controls.

Kevin Pho: Now, what did you see at this conference? What are some of the new tactics that drug makers are using to market to physicians?

Martha Rosenberg: OK, well the first one, of course, is AI. They have new apps which are called agentic, meaning agent-like. They bypass a lot of the slow approval rules as far as getting a new drug on the market.

But secondly, they very much perceive how a health care provider feels about a certain drug. For example, at the conference they talked about how health care providers were annoyed when they had met with a rep and then they get introduced to the drug information. And it’s like, “Don’t you know where I am on the journey?”

They call it the journey, the prescription journey. So the AI apps would perceive where this prescriber might be in terms of the goal of getting them to prescribe. That was the use of AI.

Drug makers have very much changed the language, and every time you hear “journey,” it’s big pharma. They talk about your health care journey if you’re the patient. But they also talk about the prescription journey for the health care provider. So there’s a lot of machinations over how these drugs are marketed.

One other thing I wrote about right before this was that increasingly they’re targeting lab workers to market drugs, because they want to reach a patient or a practitioner early in the prescription journey.

Kevin Pho: All right, so AI, of course, using these agentic tools. So as a physician, how would they know that they’re the target of an agentic marketing tool? What would that look like to them?

Martha Rosenberg: Wow, I love that question, and I don’t really know. I’ve personally received phone calls from AI, so I don’t know if it’s phone-based. It’s certainly clear that we’re being spied upon, including me as a reporter. But how would it look? I would guess it would be a very tailored message.

“We know that you wrote this article last week,” or “We know that you pulled these side effects,” so it would be very precise in terms of what the prescriber has done or is doing. Certainly if the prescriber is involved in clinical trials, that would be, “We know that you’re researching this.” But it would be just very targeted to specific facts that are going on.

Kevin Pho: And as far as you know, and I know that we’re really early into this agentic era, in terms of the effectiveness of this, do you have any data or any insight in terms of how effective AI or agentic marketing is?

Martha Rosenberg: Not from the standpoint of the prescribers, but certainly when you look at Wall Street and you look at drug prices, you look at GLP-1 agonists, it’s obvious that this kind of AI marketing is larger than life, and so we know it’s very effective. And one thing that I write about is how health care costs and tax dollars are affected by this.

Kevin Pho: All right. So in your article you wrote about three new pharma marketing tactics, and we talked about AI, so what are the other new pharma marketing tactics we should be aware of?

Martha Rosenberg: Sure. Well, this is not necessarily new, but it was confirmed at the conference, and as a reporter it irritates me a lot, and this would be disease mongering. We make a joke in my area about, you know, do you fall asleep at night and wake up in the morning? You might be suffering from something. So this whole idea of, whoever you are, you might be sick.

They had a seminar at this conference about new disease marketing, and they literally said, they’re not even hiding it, quote, “It creates new markets. We’re redefining education. We’re rewriting the playbook of engagement with prescribers.” So they admit that they’re using disease fears to make money.

Kevin Pho: So what does that look like, disease mongering? Would it just be bringing awareness to a relatively rare disease, or simply talking about it? What does that look like?

Martha Rosenberg: Well, that’s a great question. Disease mongering began with symptom checkers and websites for “Do you have EPI?” or “Do you have depression?” or “Do you have pain?” How could somebody not know if they had pain or depression? But anyway, it began with what they would call awareness.

Then it segued to what we now see, which is influencers sharing their story. One thing we’ve seen a lot in reporting is, quote unquote, “My story really sells.” Somebody says, “Well, I had diabetes.” There are more than 3 million health influencers on TikTok, and so that’s another form of disease mongering that we see.

Another thing, Dr. Pho, is that even general interest magazines, old-fashioned glossy magazines in the bookstore, now monger. “Are you on the spectrum? Are you an adult with ADHD?” So what I’ve seen as a reporter for 20 years is that there’s some kind of sales magic that happens when people self-diagnose with an elusive disease that doesn’t really have parameters.

There are so many of these self-diagnosed conditions. So disease mongering is literally selling a disease. It’s an excuse. Maybe you were late to work, but you might have this mental illness. It’s an excuse, it’s an identity, and it’s certainly a path to sell drugs.

Kevin Pho: Now, you mentioned the role of health care influencers, especially on social media sites like TikTok. Now, as a patient, how would they know that these influencers are sometimes sponsored or paid for by pharma? Are they required to do any disclosures?

Martha Rosenberg: I can’t answer that one, because I don’t watch them. I give them wide berth. I would guess no. But a lot of people have a personality as a podcaster, and of course we know they have a lot of advertisers, and I don’t think they really say, “Well, I’m paid by so-and-so.” I don’t think they do, but I really can’t answer that, because I just avoid them.

I will say this: When I’m here in Evanston, on the Northwestern campus, and you go into the medical waiting rooms, you see what look like magazines that are actually pharma communications designed to look like magazines. So that’s influencing. But as far as the podcasters, I can’t tell you that.

One thing I do know from being in this field for a while is that the ultimate sales energy is from friends, and social media figured this out a long time ago. If your friends are eating this or wearing this or saying this, that will influence people. So certainly with social influencers, if you look a certain way, you want to be like her. I would guess that the social influencers are more effective than even what they do with the prescribers, because you relate to them.

Kevin Pho: Now, you wrote in your article that in Maryland, for instance, there’s a bill that would force disclosure of pharma funding for some of these disease awareness campaigns. Now, tell us more about that.

Martha Rosenberg: OK, so now I don’t know the fate of this bill, but last month a bill was introduced in Maryland to force disclosure of pharma funding. The part that I’m intrigued with is that a lot of so-called patient advocacy groups are funded by big pharma. So they would be forced to say, “Well, 70 percent of our funding comes in from pharma.” The bill would try to separate what’s really medicine from what’s hype and marketing.

I feel naturally there’s going to be antipathy against that, because so many of our lawmakers federally are funded by big pharma, including their reelection campaigns.

Kevin Pho: The other distinction that you made in your article that I found interesting was a shift from direct-to-consumer advertising to direct-to-patient marketing. So give us a sense of what exactly that distinction is and why that’s important going forward.

Martha Rosenberg: Well, that’s a very important point in the article and at the conference, because we’ve seen direct-to-consumer ads for more than 20 years, the ones that say “ask your doctor.” The move from drug makers in that sector is to direct-to-patient, which would be, as we talked about, pharma-funded practices. Sometimes they’re in strip malls. A lot of times they’re on the internet, and they have nothing to do with a hospital or actual medicine.

We hear a lot about PBMs and the cost. What I’m seeing here in Chicago is that the CVSes and the Walgreens are circling the drain because pharma’s going direct to the patients. So direct-to-patient, I don’t know if the motive is to bypass the FDA, but it certainly has the effect of bypassing the FDA, because we know the FDA will not really allow incorrect ads or marketing.

So direct-to-patient would be just grabbing their space and, you know, there’s an instant, we know on the internet people like instant results. It’s like, “See a doctor now about your insomnia, and get your drug tomorrow.” Well, the FDA, as I’ve worked with them, doesn’t want that. That’s snake oil, you know?

Kevin Pho: So are we talking about bypassing physicians and offering tests? What are some examples of this direct-to-patient marketing that you’re talking about?

Martha Rosenberg: Well, that would be disease mongering to sell drugs. In other words, I see this sometimes on the internet. “Are you on the spectrum? Talk to a doctor now. We can get your medication tomorrow.” The bypassing, Dr. Pho, would be things like just giving you a questionnaire rather than an office visit, and certainly the prescriber is paid by the drug company. There’s no mystery about that.

When you see these little offices, they’re pop-ups. They’re pop-up drug sales offices. All the material and the pamphlets are from GSK or from Eli Lilly or Merck. So there’s not really an attempt to pretend to be with a hospital or a practice.

Kevin Pho: Now, is there a case that some of this less overt pharma marketing can be helpful in keeping physicians up to date on some of the latest drugs and treatments and diagnostic paths? Because, as you know, doctors are busy, and sometimes they aren’t able to keep up to date on the latest journals. And sometimes this information, being less overtly pharma-branded, is there a legitimate educational component? Can that case be made at all?

Martha Rosenberg: Well, you make a good point. I think the lack of time that prescribers have is a real factor in both selling and knowledge. I would say, I hate to say this, Dr. Pho, but a lot of news outlets have now grabbed onto journal news, and the journal says this drug prevents dementia, and it’s the clinical trial, and it’s just a surrogate endpoint anyway. But the clinical trial was sponsored by a drug maker, and that news byte will be presented by outlets as news.

So my worry is that prescribers hear that and they think, “Oh my goodness.” Well, that’s marketing. That’s just marketing. So in answer to your question, I would tell anyone who is a prescriber, including nurses and nurse practitioners, to go to their peers and peer groups, because that would be more free from the marketing influences.

Kevin Pho: We’re talking to Martha Rosenberg. She’s an investigative reporter. Today’s KevinMD article is “Three new pharma marketing tactics every physician should know.” Martha, as always, let’s end with some of your take-home messages that you want to leave with the KevinMD audience.

Martha Rosenberg: Oh, thank you, Dr. Pho. I would just ask prescribers and patients to be cynical and skeptical of all the messages they get, especially when they’re frenzied and overnight and dramatic and breaking news. Be cynical, because really good medicine, as you know, takes a while. It’s not overnight news. So I’d say be skeptical, be cynical. The selling that’s going on now is very stealthy.

Kevin Pho: Martha, thank you so much for sharing your perspective and insight, and thanks again for coming back on the show.

Martha Rosenberg: Thank you. Thank you.

title: The life hack that could undo medical debt credit reports
summary: “I just don’t pay them.” I was with a group of acquaintances, and we had been engaged in a spirited conversation about the costs of medical care. While I was the only one present who...
full_content:
“I just don’t pay them.”

I was with a group of acquaintances, and we had been engaged in a spirited conversation about the costs of medical care. While I was the only one present who worked in health care, the group itself was fairly homogenous, with individuals in similar stages of life and financial security. Access to health insurance was of no concern in this group, and neither would have been out-of-pocket expenses. When the conversation inevitably drifted to complaints about the rising costs of that care, one person described a new practice that they had recently adopted. A “life hack,” they called it. It was the “life hack” of not paying any of their medical bills.

There is a whole culture now built upon using “life hacks” to get ahead. TikTok videos and savvy podcast hosts describe countless practices from “credit card churning” and soliciting service retention offers all the way to “manufactured spending” and “skiplagging.” Some of these practices are shrewd and socially accepted, while others reside in the gray zones in the terms of service. Regardless of where each of these practices lies on an ethical spectrum, they seem to be increasing in popularity among my age peers, frustrated by rising costs and an uncertain economic outlook.

But their admission, almost a boast, of nonpayment, struck me immediately. It was said without guilt or remorse, even in the presence of me, a physician! And no one else in the conversation pushed back on the practice. I wondered, “Why would a group of typically ethically forward individuals generally agree that a calculated failure to pay medical bills was acceptable?” Especially when they all had the financial capacity to easily do so.

As surprised as I had been when I first learned of this practice, I have now been present on two separate occasions, and with separate groups, where this “life hack” was given as a tutorial. Some described the practice of paying medical bills only after they have gone to collections and then paying the collection agency a fraction of the original bill. For others, the mechanism is to simply not worry even after they are sent to collections since medical debt is treated differently on credit reports and therefore any unresolved judgments are less likely to cause financial consequences. The common theme was less about the decision itself than the framing. By labeling the practice as a “life hack,” there was no consideration about the ethical implications. While premeditated failure to pay for non-health care goods and services would likely receive strong societal condemnation, why do ethics seem to be suspended when this is done for medical care?

Economists have observed similar behaviors before. During the late 2000s financial crisis, the strongest predictor of who would walk away from an underwater mortgage they could afford wasn’t the size of the loss, but moral conviction and recognition of the practice. People who thought strategic default was ethically wrong were 77 percent less likely to say they’d do it. And knowing someone who’d strategically defaulted made people 82 percent more likely to say they would do it too. While not identical scenarios, this information is instructive for our consideration of strategic failure to pay medical debt. Like strategic defaulting, it likely spreads through conversations, one table and one Reddit thread at a time. I have now been at three of those tables.

Now, I want to be clear as there is a real crisis of medical debt in the United States. Approximately one in five Americans carries medical debt, and the vast majority is involuntary and the byproduct of some emergency or life-changing diagnosis. Furthermore, the cost of medical care continues to rise, and does so at a time when many are losing access to affordable health insurance. They are left with few options in times of crisis. As the popularity of high-deductible Health Savings Account (HSA)-eligible health plans continues to increase, more individuals are responsible for a greater portion of their care out-of-pocket.

Consumer advocacy groups and legislative bodies recognize the harm medical debt causes in our society and various policies have been implemented to address the issue. In 2022, the three major credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) announced they would remove medical debts less than $500, delay reporting for a grace period of one year after the debt became delinquent, and remove paid debt from credit reports. Seventeen states have passed legislation protecting residents from medical debt, with many restricting medical debts from consumer credit reports. In January 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) finalized a nationwide rule that would have banned medical debt from credit reports or being used in credit decisions. However, this rule was vacated by a federal court later that year when CFPB declined to defend the new rule when it was challenged in court.

Those patchwork protections rest on an empirical claim, but a valid one. When the CFPB examined five million credit records, it found that people carrying medical collections defaulted less often than their credit scores would have predicted. Medical debt seems to be more of a record that something happened to an individual, and not a reliable indicator of whether a person will pay their mortgage or car loan. Every piece of legitimate advocacy guidance carries the premise that it is intended to benefit those who cannot afford to pay. Charity care is means-tested by design. But while advice travels, the premise does not necessarily travel with it.

That is what makes this “life hack” a gaming of the system rather than a loophole. While it might seem to be a victimless practice, there are consequences. And there is a fundamental difference between medical debt due to inability to pay versus medical debt due to deliberate failure to do so. This is a conscious, voluntary action. And the concern is that every solvent defector, including each of my acquaintances, is a small argument against these credit protections. And groups looking to put medical debt back on credit reports are looking for exactly that argument.

We now have some idea of how often patients pay what they owe, and the answer is unsettling. Health economists found that repayment of owed cost sharing (the cost attributed to patients that includes deductibles and co-pays, and is the cost my acquaintances were declining to pay) was roughly 54 percent before the pandemic and has fallen since then. This proportion is somewhat misleading, however, since they also showed that in over 90 percent of cases, patients paid either all or none of the liability. While this is not a causal relationship, the pattern seems to be less consistent with financial hardship, which would likely include more partial payments or negotiated installments, than a conscious decision to decline payment of bills. Furthermore, the proportional decline they saw was driven not by patients paying smaller portions of their bills, but by a larger share of patients paying nothing at all. More dinner table conversations. More Reddit posts.

Unpaid liability is a cost to hospitals and physicians, and hospitals are not helpless. While it is becoming more common to require prepayment for elective medical care, it would never be an appropriate practice to enact prepayments of emergent care. And what barriers would systemic prepayment requirements produce when enacted in nonelective primary and specialty care?

Truthfully, unpaid patient liability represents less than 10 percent of expected payments for both inpatient and outpatient care among privately insured patients. And even if every solvent professional in America ceased paying their portion of medical care tomorrow, the system could potentially absorb the shock. But this was never about the money itself. The answer here is not to put medical debt back on credit reports. What is being spent down is not hospital revenue, but the small, very recent, hard-won agreement that getting sick is not a moral failure and that the bill which follows should not be read like one. It took decades of advocacy to win that agreement; we cannot let it be compromised by a “life hack.”

Dan Pierce is a physiatrist.

title: Cookbook medicine and the loss of clinical judgment
summary: “The brain is a wonderful organ. It starts working the moment you get up in the morning and does not stop until you get into the office.” – Robert Frost Since the publication of my f...
full_content:
“The brain is a wonderful organ. It starts working the moment you get up in the morning and does not stop until you get into the office.”
– Robert Frost

Since the publication of my first nonfiction book, Failure to Treat: How a Broken Healthcare System Puts Patients and Practitioners at Risk, I have been deluged with medical stories. In fact, nearly everyone who has read the book has been anxious to tell me about cases that have adversely affected themselves or someone in their family. Their stories have common themes, many having to do with cost or availability of care. But perhaps what has been most frustrating have been situations in which there is powerful evidence that medical professionals in whom they placed their trust simply failed to use their brain.

The most recent example came from one of my medical school roommates. Patrick is a retired and highly successful endocrinologist, reputed for his thorough and thoughtful care. His brother, Myles, had recently seen his primary care doctor because he noticed swelling in his ankles. Without explaining why, the physician told Myles it could be heart failure, and he would need to see a cardiologist. When Patrick called the office to obtain more information for his anxious brother, he was put on the phone not with the doctor who saw Myles, but with his nurse practitioner. She could find no evidence in the chart that a physical examination had been performed or that pertinent laboratory work had been ordered. She could only state that the doctor had been worried about heart failure and referred the patient to a cardiologist to have him “checked out.”

Over the last few decades, medical knowledge has exploded. Thousands of clinical trials have enabled the approval of hundreds of new drugs and devices. Through no fault of their own, clinicians are struggling to keep up. Increasing time in the office means less time to read and attend conferences. Primary care doctors have been under particular pressure. Whereas consultants can focus their attention on a few circumscribed topics, generalists are expected to know something about every disease and organ system. These beleaguered people try to keep their head above water by reading top-line data on the internet.

In their clinical practice, generalists have become increasingly dependent on algorithms. The “If you see this, then do that” approach has become commonplace, particularly among physician associates. Professional organizations have unwittingly contributed by publishing “guidelines” for just about every disease. Though intended to provide up-to-date information, guidelines have been misinterpreted as the standard of care. They have been condensed into diagrams so naive practitioners can select a test or treatment regardless of the individual patient’s profile. Fear of malpractice, another dramatic factor in the denigration of medical care, further motivates primary care practitioners to refer anyone with anything other than a routine problem to a specialist to avoid being sued for a bad outcome. Myles, a diabetic with a positive family history of cardiac disease, was shipped posthaste to a cardiologist without even the most rudimentary work-up that might have revealed an innocent reason for swollen ankles.

Opening more medical schools and using community hospitals for teaching residents and students, though necessary to increase the supply of doctors of all specialties, will dilute the quality of the educational experience even further. Nurse practitioners and physician assistants, extremely valuable associates, are tossed into practice situations for which they are not fully prepared. And throwing gasoline on the fire, our politicians have decided that all will be well when artificial intelligence takes over, when AI will only replicate the robotic behavior of poorly trained practitioners. Despite heavy criticism, AI is being put into place to determine if a test or treatment ordered by a physician will be approved for payment by Medicare.

Medicine is an art form, learned from experienced mentors over many years through direct patient experience. When practiced correctly, it is arguably the most intellectually and emotionally challenging human endeavor. Compassionate and skilled primary care practitioners are in great demand but also underpaid and under siege. Given the avalanche of new medical information, it is certainly reasonable to provide these overworked practitioners with a scaffold of reliable, evidence-based recommendations that they can use as a general guide. But that information always needs to be placed into the context of individual patient needs and expectations as well as concomitant conditions and overall prognosis. It is up to all health care professionals to make sure that cookbook medicine practiced by robots never happens. There is simply too much at stake.

Peter R. Kowey is professor of medicine and clinical pharmacology at Thomas Jefferson University, emeritus chief of the division of cardiovascular diseases at the Lankenau Heart Institute, and the William Wikoff Smith Chair in Cardiovascular Research at the Lankenau Institute for Medical Research.

Dr. Kowey is an internationally recognized expert in heart rhythm disorders. His research, regulatory, and clinical trial expertise have led to the development of innovative therapies for cardiac arrhythmias. He is the recipient of more than 150 grants, has written more than 450 papers and scientific reports, and has coedited five textbooks on cardiac arrhythmia. He has trained hundreds of fellows who practice cardiology and cardiac electrophysiology around the world.

Dr. Kowey is a fellow of the American Heart Association, the American College of Cardiology, the American College of Physicians, and the Heart Rhythm Society, along with several other professional organizations. He was a member of the Cardio-Renal Drug Advisory Committee and the Cardiovascular Devices Advisory Committee of the Food and Drug Administration. He has received numerous awards, including the Edward S. Cooper Award from the American Heart Association and the William Osler Award from the University of Miami.

Dr. Kowey is a graduate of St. Joseph’s University and the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine. He completed his residency training in internal medicine at Penn State University and was a fellow in cardiovascular medicine and research at the Harvard University School of Public Health, the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, and the West Roxbury VA Hospital. He has published six novels and is the author of the upcoming book Failure to Treat: How a Broken Healthcare System Puts Patients and Providers at Risk. He shares updates on Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, and Substack.

title: 7 ways to use AI for better health and nutrition
summary: Like many doctors, I was initially skeptical about artificial intelligence (AI). As a retired Australian anesthetist, I had spent decades relying on clinical experience, scientific evidence, and profe...
full_content:
Like many doctors, I was initially skeptical about artificial intelligence (AI). As a retired Australian anesthetist, I had spent decades relying on clinical experience, scientific evidence, and professional judgment. I never imagined that one of the most useful health education tools I would encounter would be a mobile phone.

In 2024, I was living with obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea, and gastric reflux. Like many people, I accepted these conditions as part of aging and expected that more medications might be needed over time.

Alongside my health care team, I began using ChatGPT to better understand nutrition, lifestyle medicine, and metabolic health. Artificial intelligence did not treat my medical conditions. It educated me.

It helped me understand scientific papers, evaluate nutrition claims, interpret health information, and ask better questions. Most importantly, it helped me become a more informed participant in my own health care.

Over the following two years, I experienced significant improvements in my health. I lost substantial weight, achieved remission of type 2 diabetes, normalized my blood pressure without medication, and experienced major improvements in reflux and sleep-related symptoms.

My experience may not be typical, and I am not suggesting that artificial intelligence can replace health care professionals. However, it made me realize that AI has the potential to become one of the most powerful health education tools ever available to ordinary people.

Through our YouEatSafely health education project, we have explored practical ways members of the public can use AI to improve their health knowledge and lifestyle:

  • Reading food labels: Many consumers struggle to understand ingredient lists and nutrition panels. A person can simply photograph a food label and ask ChatGPT to explain ingredients, protein content, fiber content, added sugars, and food additives in plain language. Instead of relying solely on marketing claims, consumers can make more informed decisions about what they buy.
  • Analyzing meals: A photograph of a meal can start a conversation about nutrition. ChatGPT can identify major food groups, comment on protein sources, recognize vegetables, and suggest areas for improvement. The purpose is not to achieve perfection but to increase awareness.
  • Suggesting healthier food choices: After analyzing a meal, users can ask how it might be improved. AI can suggest practical changes such as increasing protein intake, adding vegetables, reducing sugary drinks, increasing fiber, or including fermented foods. Small improvements sustained over time often have greater impact than dramatic dietary changes that are difficult to maintain.
  • Navigating restaurant menus: Many individuals find it difficult to make healthy choices when dining out. By analyzing a menu, ChatGPT can help identify options that align with personal goals, whether that involves increasing protein intake, reducing processed foods, or improving overall dietary quality.
  • Improving health literacy: Medical information can be difficult to understand. Patients frequently leave consultations with unanswered questions or struggle to interpret health information they encounter online. ChatGPT can explain common medical conditions, blood test results, nutrition concepts, and health news using language that is easier to understand. Better understanding often leads to better conversations with health care professionals.
  • Interactive HealthCards: This application is one that particularly excites us. Traditional health education is largely passive. People read a leaflet, watch a video, or attend a lecture, but there is often little interaction. To address this problem, we have developed simple Interactive HealthCards. Each card contains a health message and a short self-assessment checklist. Users read the card, tick the boxes that apply to them, and then upload the card to ChatGPT. For example, they might write, “I uploaded this HealthCard and ticked boxes 1, 3 and 5. What can I do to improve?” ChatGPT can then provide personalized educational feedback, practical suggestions, and motivational guidance. The interaction remains private, immediate, and available at any time. In our experience, this transforms health education from passive reading into active learning.
  • Breaking the language barrier: This addresses one of the greatest barriers to health education worldwide. Many people do not speak English as their first language. Others struggle with medical terminology, even in their native language. Through our International Health Education Help Desk, people can ask questions in their preferred language and receive explanations they can better understand. AI-powered translation and communication tools have the potential to make health education accessible to communities that have traditionally been underserved.

Taken together, these seven applications suggest a new direction for health education. The greatest opportunity may not be that AI can answer questions. Rather, it is that AI can transform health education from a one-way transfer of information into an interactive conversation. For the first time, a mobile phone can help people learn, reflect, self-assess, improve their lifestyle, and access health education in their own language.

Artificial intelligence should never replace doctors, nurses, dietitians, or other health care professionals. However, it can help people become more informed participants in their own health care.

The goal is simple: to help people better understand their health, improve their lifestyle, and work with their health care professionals to achieve the best possible outcomes. If used responsibly, AI may prove to be one of the most important health education tools of our time.

Siva Navaratnam is a retired anesthesiologist in Australia. Shimazu Yumi is a health care executive.

title: 麦科医药MT200605完成II期临床锁库，脑梗神经“护修”疗法即将揭盲
summary: 麦科医药自主研发的急性缺血性卒中（脑梗）创新药MT200605完成II期临床数据库锁定，即将揭盲与统计分析。该研究入组360例患者，仅用时约5.5个月。脑梗致残率高，目前治疗手段有限，MT200605是唯一进入临床阶段、靶向BDNF\u002FTrkB神经营养通路的神经营养类脑梗药物，主张“护修并举”，可减少神经细胞死亡，促进神经再生。数据库锁定意味着研究结果可靠性得到保障，麦科医药将在揭盲后全面...
full_content:
近日，麦科医药宣布，其自主研发的急性缺血性卒中（脑梗）创新药MT200605的II期临床研究正式完成数据库锁定，即将进入揭盲与统计分析阶段。该研究共入组360例患者，从首例入组到全部完成仅用时约5.5个月。


脑梗是全球致残率最高的疾病之一。全球每年新发1200万例，550万人因此离世。中国每年新增409万例，约70%～80%的幸存者留有偏瘫、失语等严重后遗症。目前溶栓与取栓虽能开通血管，但因时间窗严格、识别延迟等因素，仅少数患者能及时接受治疗，多数人只能被动依赖保守治疗。


MT200605是一款可高效穿透血脑屏障的小分子静脉注射液，靶向BDNF/TrkB神经营养通路，是目前唯一进入临床阶段、具有该机制的神经营养类脑梗药物。其设计思路区别于传统单一抗氧化药物，主张“护修并举”：一方面清除氧自由基、抑制凋亡和炎症，减少神经细胞死亡；另一方面激活TrkB受体，下达内源性修复指令，促进突触重塑和神经再生，为长期功能恢复铺路。


数据库锁定是临床试验的关键里程碑，意味着全部数据已完成核查和审核，研究结果可靠性得到保障。麦科医药表示，将在揭盲后全面评估MT200605的有效性与安全性，并据此制定III期确证性研究方案。


1986年诺贝尔奖曾揭示神经生长因子的存在，证明神经元可被“滋养”与“修复”。MT200605正是这一科学脉络在脑梗治疗领域的最新探索。若后续研究取得积极结果，有望为高危致残的脑梗后遗症提供全新的主动干预路径。

title: 里程碑 | 中国首家！简达生物新一代重组流感疫苗获FDA临床批件
summary: 过去半个多世纪，鸡胚培养成流感疫苗生产重要技术路线，但其在抗原匹配、生产周期等方面有局限，流感病毒持续变异及需求变化使其面临优化空间。全球流感疫苗产业期待技术突破，流感疫苗市场规模约80亿美元，长期稳定接种需求下，技术领先者将占优势。简达生物选择重组蛋白技术路线，其自主研发的新一代重组蛋白流感疫苗JD02获美国食品药品监督管理局（FDA）临床试验批件，正式进入美国临床开发阶段。该疫苗通过基因工程技...
full_content:
过去半个多世纪，人类对抗流感病毒的方式，绕不开一枚鸡蛋。

 

自上世纪40年代以来，鸡胚培养逐渐成为流感疫苗生产的重要技术路线。但随着流感病毒持续变异以及疫苗供应需求不断变化，传统鸡胚培养路线在抗原匹配、生产周期等方面面临进一步优化空间。

 

在这一背景下，中国创新疫苗企业也开始探索新的技术路径。

 

近日，简达生物宣布，其自主研发的新一代重组蛋白流感疫苗JD02获得美国食品药品监督管理局（FDA）临床试验批件，正式进入美国临床开发阶段。


 

流感疫苗并不是一个新兴赛道。

 

相比近年来快速发展的HPV疫苗、带状疱疹疫苗等创新疫苗领域，流感疫苗已经形成成熟的产业体系。但由于流感病毒具有持续变异特点，疫苗保护并非一次接种即可长期维持，而需要根据全球流行毒株变化进行周期性更新，因此形成了长期稳定的接种需求。

 

这也意味着，谁能在技术上实现突破，谁就能在这个稳定的大市场中占据长期优势。

 

从市场规模来看，流感疫苗已经成为全球疫苗产业的重要组成部分。根据Global Market Insights数据，全球流感疫苗市场规模约80亿美元。

 

长期以来，鸡胚培养是流感疫苗生产的重要方式。该方法通过在鸡胚中扩增流感病毒，再经过灭活、纯化等工艺制备疫苗，具有成熟度高、产业化经验丰富等特点。

 

但随着流感病毒变异速度加快以及全球公共卫生需求变化，传统鸡胚培养路线的一些局限逐渐受到关注。

 

其中，抗原匹配问题是行业长期关注的挑战之一。由于流感病毒需要在鸡胚环境中进行扩增，在这一过程中可能发生适应性突变，使疫苗生产株与实际流行株之间产生一定差异，进而影响疫苗免疫保护效果。

 

此外，鸡胚培养依赖稳定的鸡胚供应体系，生产流程相对复杂，传统工艺的生产周期长达6个月，一旦出现流感大流行，无法快速扩产以匹配激增的防疫需求。

 

简达生物董事长周明在采访中直言：“鸡胚培养带来的适应性（基因）突变导致最终疫苗产品与人群流行毒株不匹配，从而导致目前市面场上使用的流感疫苗普遍低效甚至无效。”

 

正是在这一背景下，全球流感疫苗产业开始探索新的技术路径，希望通过新的生产体系提升抗原设计能力和生产灵活性。



 

在全球流感疫苗技术不断演进的背景下，简达生物选择了重组蛋白技术路线。

 

与传统依赖病毒扩增获得抗原的生产方式不同，重组蛋白疫苗通过基因工程技术直接表达病毒关键抗原，从而减少生产过程中病毒适应性变化带来的影响。

 

在JD02研发过程中，简达生物采用Sf9昆虫细胞表达系统生产流感病毒血凝素（HA）抗原，并结合自主研发的佐剂体系，开发三价重组蛋白流感疫苗。根据FDA IND文件，JD02为三价重组流感蛋白疫苗，包含针对甲型流感病毒亚型及乙型流感病毒的抗原成分。

 

对于重组蛋白疫苗而言，抗原设计和免疫增强能力是决定产品竞争力的重要因素。

 

简达生物通过优化抗原设计，提高疫苗诱导免疫反应的能力。公司团队表示，JD02通过新的抗原设计策略以及佐剂体系，希望同时增强体液免疫和细胞免疫反应。

 

此次FDA临床批件的含金量，体现在审评过程的一次性通过。根据FDA官方邮件，简达生物于2026年6月9日正式递交IND原始申请，7月8日收到FDA的避免临床暂停沟通（avoid hold communication），公司在24小时内完成回复，7月9日即收到FDA确认函。整个过程中，FDA未要求补充任何数据资料。

 

 

流感疫苗只是简达生物布局的第一步。

 

围绕创新疫苗研发，公司正在构建覆盖预防性疫苗和治疗性疫苗的产品体系。

 

在研发策略上，简达生物关注具有长期市场需求、同时存在技术升级空间的疾病领域。公司团队表示，疫苗项目选择主要围绕三个维度展开：市场需求、技术创新空间以及全球化开发潜力。

 

目前，公司已形成多梯度产品布局。其中，JD02重组三价流感疫苗已获得FDA IND批准，进入海外临床开发阶段；重组带状疱疹疫苗也已进入II期临床；此外，公司还布局了2针法狂犬疫苗、抗耐药性细菌感染治疗性疫苗等方向。

 

资金方面，简达生物已完成近亿元Pre-A轮融资。本轮资金将主要用于JD02海内外临床推进、带状疱疹疫苗后续开发以及中试生产基地建设。

 

简达生物在本次专访中披露，未来公司计划继续推进JD02海外临床研究，同时寻求与国内外药企开展联合开发及商业化合作，加速创新疫苗产品向市场转化。

 

从全球市场来看，重组蛋白流感疫苗已证明了技术可行性，但这一领域仍处于持续发展阶段。未来，如何进一步提升免疫保护效果、扩大适用人群，并建立规模化生产能力，将成为企业竞争的重要方向。

 

对于中国市场而言，目前重组蛋白流感疫苗仍处于研发推进阶段，尚未形成成熟商业化产品。但近两年，国内第三代重组蛋白流感疫苗研发明显加速，多家企业相继进入临床阶段。但从实验室研发走向商业化，仍需要经历临床数据验证、生产体系建设以及全球市场拓展等多个环节。

 

国内重组蛋白流感疫苗在研管线

 

在一个拥有长期接种需求的成熟疫苗市场中，下一轮竞争或许不只是围绕“生产一款疫苗”，而是围绕抗原设计能力、免疫技术平台以及全球商业化能力展开。

title: What becoming a chief medical officer taught a shy doctor
summary: I never sought out leadership. It found me. We met when I clumsily stumbled into it as a junior faculty. Razor-focused on patient care and teaching, I stared at my clinical leader with bewilderment wh...
full_content:
I never sought out leadership. It found me. We met when I clumsily stumbled into it as a junior faculty. Razor-focused on patient care and teaching, I stared at my clinical leader with bewilderment when she asked me if I had thought about becoming an associate program director. While I questioned whether I had the experience or qualifications, I took on the role, and found deep fulfillment and joy in it. A few years later, I gave my department chair a quizzical look when he asked if I would consider becoming vice chair of clinical operations. The broken record of self-doubt played its scratchy tune in my mind as I pondered whether I really had the skills to take on such a role; I eventually did, and grew as a leader under his tutelage and through my experiences leading an exceptional team.

Years later, multiple mentors tapped my shoulder again about the opportunity to serve as chief medical officer (CMO) of our clinical practice. This time, I didn’t even turn the record on. Instead, I laughed out loud and shook my head. And yet, with ongoing prodding and encouragement, I applied for the role of a lifetime and used all that I had learned from previous experiences to hit the ground running as a CMO in 2022. Wide-eyed and wary, I read voraciously and leaned on trusted teachers for guidance and support. I jotted down my notes into a journal which evolved into a book, The Leadership Learning Curve: A Woman Physician’s Journey as a Chief Medical Officer.

Why is it that I didn’t see myself as a leader? And why is it the same for so many physicians I know? I am not alone in my narratives that consistently ended with, “I was encouraged to apply, so I did.” When I think back on my medical training, leadership development was not integrated into the curriculum. The natural leaders were the high scorers on tests, outspoken, and with prowess to command a room. Over time, I equated these characteristics with leadership. As the shy, introverted girl who was often labeled as quiet, I quickly categorized myself as a non-leader.

In hindsight, the leaders who inspired me and who I continue to try to emulate were not defined by traits, but more by their ability to achieve a goal while transforming others around them in the process. They listened, cared, were vulnerable, paid close attention to the data, took ownership of mistakes, amplified successes of the team, and never lost sight of the mission. They asked the tough questions, embraced uncertainty, and knew how to get to the heart of any matter with compassion and grace. I like to think that it’s these practices that my leaders saw in me, more than I recognized on my own.

Part of my purpose in writing The Leadership Learning Curve was to ensure future CMOs would not have to do the cognitive legwork I did to piece together vital information about health care, finance, and leading a team. On a deeper level, I wanted to give physicians like me who self-categorized as non-leaders a glimpse into the world of health care leadership, and show how leadership is built on a foundation of trust and building relationships with a genuine commitment to lifelong learning.

We need physicians in health care leadership. Nobody knows our patients, our colleagues, our teams, or the complex problems of health care in granular detail more than we do. As physicians, committing to leadership development goes hand in hand with keeping up with the latest literature in our fields; as leaders and as physicians, we are in the practice of caring for people. It is in the genuine caring for people that we grow and transform ourselves. This is why I am proud to serve as secretary of the American Medical Women’s Association (AMWA), an organization that recognizes the vital importance of developing physician leaders. AMWA offers premier leadership programs like EVOLVE for residents and fellows, and ELEVATE for physicians, paving the way for women physicians to not only see themselves as leaders, but also develop the skills to thrive. On a personal note, it was my AMWA community that helped me find my voice and build my confidence to lead.

Whether you are an intern finding your footing in clinical care or a junior faculty wondering if you could ever be a leader, I hope you find inspiration from this book to pursue leadership in health care. Time to throw away the broken record.

Vidhya Prakash, MD, is the associate dean of clinical affairs and population health and chief medical officer at SIU Medicine in Springfield, Illinois. She is also a professor of clinical internal medicine and serves on the infectious diseases faculty.

Her work centers on physician leadership development, with a particular focus on adaptive leadership. She is deeply committed to community engagement and to advancing solutions that address health disparities.

She is the author of Leadership Learning Curve and Learning to Listen. She is a proud fellow of the American College of Physicians, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the American Medical Women’s Association (AMWA), where she currently serves as secretary. She shares updates on LinkedIn.

The American Medical Women’s Association (AMWA) is the oldest multispecialty organization dedicated to advancing women physicians and improving the health of women. For more than a century, AMWA has been the vision and voice of women in medicine, pursuing its mission through leadership, advocacy, education, mentorship, and strategic partnerships.

AMWA has a long publishing history. Its members produced a series of consumer health references in the 1990s, including The Women’s Complete Health Book (Delacorte Press, 1995), the AMWA Guide to Pregnancy and Childbirth (1996), the AMWA Guide to Cardiovascular Health (1997), and The Complete Family Health Book (1999). The association’s flagship scholarly publication, the Journal of the American Medical Women’s Association (JAMWA), ran from 1946 to 2005 and grew out of earlier titles that trace back to the Bulletin of the Medical Women’s National Association, first published in 1922.

AMWA shares updates on LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, X, and Bluesky.

title: The people-pleasing in medicine that burns doctors out
summary: We are taught from the first days of medical school that bedside manner is a clinical tool as vital as a stethoscope. We are told to listen, to mirror, and to connect. But for many of us, this directi...
full_content:
We are taught from the first days of medical school that bedside manner is a clinical tool as vital as a stethoscope. We are told to listen, to mirror, and to connect. But for many of us, this directive has quietly morphed into a high-stakes performance. If you find yourself leaving the exam room physically exhausted, not from the medicine, but from the emotional labor of managing patient reactions, you are likely caught in the pleasing trap.

I remember sitting in seminars hosted by malpractice carriers where the advice was always the same: listen more, validate constantly, and ensure the patient feels heard. At the time, it sounded like sound professional wisdom. But over the years, I began to see those instructions for what they often are, coded mandates for patient-pleasing behavior. We have been conditioned to interpret the noble, valid concept of “patient-centered care” as a license to prioritize patient satisfaction over clinical authority.

This is a specific, painful byproduct of the personality traits that draw many of us to medicine: high-functioning perfectionism, a touch of neuroticism, and a deep-seated need for external validation. We have built our identities around being the perfect doctor, the one who is always liked, never confrontational, and universally approved of. But there is a hidden cost to this. When we treat the patient’s approval as the primary outcome of an encounter, we are no longer just healing; we are constantly editing our clinical truth to avoid the sting of rejection.

It becomes a dangerous game. Every time we over-explain a rational decision because we fear a patient’s frustration, or offer a concession we know is medically unnecessary just to keep the peace, we are leaking energy. We are paying for their approval with our own professional integrity.

True clinical excellence is not about being a crowd-pleaser; it is about holding a boundary. The best doctors are not the ones who ensure every patient leaves happy; they are the ones who can hold space for a patient’s disappointment without internalizing it as a personal failure. They understand that their value is derived from their ethical rigor and their competence, not from a fleeting satisfaction score.

If you are constantly bracing for rejection, you aren’t actually connecting with your patients, you are managing them. And that is a recipe for a burnout that no amount of time off can fix. It is time to step off the stage. We were hired to be physicians, not actors. The most liberating thing you can do for your career is to realize that you can provide exceptional, compassionate care while being perfectly comfortable with the fact that not everyone is going to like you. Your patients will often respect you more for it, and more importantly, you will finally be able to leave the clinic with your own energy still intact.

Farid Sabet-Sharghi is a psychiatrist.s

title: 呼吸慢病全周期管理的“断层”，产业端如何填平？
summary: 《睡眠呼吸暂停和慢阻肺病诊疗及居家管理行动意见》发布，围绕两大呼吸慢病五大环节提出系统性方案。当前我国呼吸慢病治疗困境在于诊疗全周期信息断层，《行动意见》建议将治疗管理重点转向全周期连续管理。中国OSA和慢阻肺病患者众多，但公众认知不足，就诊延误，治疗依从性差，全周期管理存在鸿沟。产业端尝试用数字化手段填补“人”的缺口，“硬件+软件+平台”的闭环模式是主流探索方向，多家企业推出患者管理平台，打通院...
full_content:
近日，《睡眠呼吸暂停和慢阻肺病诊疗及居家管理行动意见》（下称《行动意见》）正式发布，由中日友好医院、医师报及项目多学科专家委员会共同编撰，围绕睡眠呼吸暂停与慢阻肺病两大呼吸慢病的早期筛查、精准诊断、规范治疗、居家管理和长期随访五大关键环节，为中国呼吸慢病管理提出了一套从“知道”到“做到”的系统性行动方案。

 

动脉了解到，当前我国睡眠呼吸暂停与慢阻肺病的治疗困境，根源可能并非“无药可治”或“无技术可用”，而是在于诊疗全周期中“无人告知、无人讲解、无人跟进”的信息断层。

 

《行动意见》建议，应将呼吸慢病的治疗管理重点从“单次诊断”转向“全周期连续管理”，通过升级居家治疗设备及远程监测等技术功能，对患者进行持续跟踪与动态管理，让患者离院不离管。

 

这一判断的背后其实是呼吸慢病防治长期面临的现实困境。

 

据统计，中国OSA（阻塞性睡眠呼吸暂停）患病人数约1.76亿，慢阻肺病患者总数逼近1亿。但调研显示，93%的受访者自称重视呼吸健康，仅1%真正掌握正确的呼吸健康常识，68%的受访者甚至认为打鼾不需要诊治。

 

《行动意见》数据显示，近半数OSA患者延误就诊超过一年，慢阻肺病患者初次确诊时病情多已处于GOLD Ⅱ级及以上，肺功能明确受损。即便跨过就诊门槛，PAP（气道正压通气）治疗3个月后能坚持规范使用的患者已不足半数。

 

从认知到诊断、从治疗到随访，每个环节都存在大量患者脱节，全周期管理的政策导向与现实之间，存在着一条亟待填补的鸿沟。

 

 

在医生资源和基层卫生服务能力短期内难以大幅提升的前提下，产业端正在尝试用数字化手段部分承担起“告知、讲解、跟进”的功能。

 

“硬件+软件+平台”的闭环模式是当前产业端的主流探索方向。

 

当前多家企业已推出面向医生端的患者管理平台，尝试打通院内诊断与居家治疗的数据链路，实现远程监测、异常预警和在线随访。这类工具的核心价值在于将患者脱离医院后的治疗行为纳入可观察、可干预的范围，让医生得以在不增加门诊量的前提下掌握患者的居家依从性和治疗效果。

 

从产业逻辑来看，设备企业有天然的动机搭建此类平台，因为设备的一次性销售收入增长空间有限，而基于数据的持续服务意味着更具黏性的用户关系和更稳定的收入结构。

 

但从实际效果来看，平台的价值高度依赖医疗端的承接能力，若医生端缺乏使用动力，平台所能产生的管理效能便十分有限。

 

在设备端，智能算法的应用正在降低患者的使用门槛。过去，呼吸机的参数设置和压力调节高度依赖专业人员现场操作，患者拿回家后因“戴不住”而放弃的比例极高。算法技术的进步使设备能够根据患者的呼吸节律自动适配压力，减少人机对抗，在客观上降低了对人工指导的依赖。

 

与此同时，电商渠道的普及和消费端补贴政策的推出，也在降低患者获得设备的成本门槛。但技术上的可及性改善，与患者是否真正理解疾病、是否愿意长期坚持治疗，仍是两个不同层面的事情。

 

 

产业方从设备供应商向管理方案共建方转型，是近年来的显著趋势，从参与临床共识制定到开展基层医生培训，企业正向医疗服务前端延伸。

 

这种延伸在基层能力薄弱、随访体系缺失的背景下有其合理性，但也面临边界问题：企业以公益身份参与共识制定，其数据与临床证据不易平衡；患者数据平台的存储、使用和安全责任归属尚缺监管框架；企业管理与医疗机构诊疗的分工亦无明确规范。

 

这些问题虽然在数字医疗领域并非独有，但在高度依赖设备长期使用的呼吸慢病专科尤为突出。

 

另一个值得关注的问题是商业模式的可持续性。国内家用呼吸机市场虽然潜力巨大，但当前体量仍然有限。

 

据测算，国内家用呼吸机市场规模约13亿元，与超过2.7亿的潜在患者基数形成强烈反差，在渗透率较低的早期市场，企业需要持续投入大量资源进行市场教育、搭建数据平台、开展基层培训。

 

这类投入带有明显的基础设施建设属性，回报周期长、不确定性高。目前这些投入多由企业以“公益支持”或“战略性投入”的名义自行承担，究竟能在多大程度上转化为可持续的商业回报，仍是行业面临的共同挑战。

 

更深层的问题在于，全周期管理的核心障碍并非技术工具的有无，而是支付机制和激励机制的设计，对于多数患者而言，一台数千元乃至上万元的设备仍是较大的经济负担，这直接制约了治疗的启动和维持。

 

与此同时，医疗机构也缺乏为出院患者提供长期随访的付费来源和绩效激励。在现行医保支付框架下，医院的服务收入主要依赖诊疗和住院环节，院外管理几乎没有收费通道，医生也缺少动力在门诊之外投入额外精力进行主动随访。

 

换言之，无人跟进的表象之下，更深层的是无法跟进的制度困境。

 

BMC瑞迈特董事长庄志进一步表示：“一台好设备只是起点，患者用不用、能不能坚持用、有没有人持续管，才是决定疗效的终点。”

 

更宏观地看，这一困境并非呼吸慢病管理独有，而是慢病管理领域普遍存在的结构性问题。随着分级诊疗和医保支付改革的推进，部分地区和病种已开始探索将院外管理纳入服务包，但从局部试点到全面推开仍有相当距离。在支付制度尚未根本性改观的条件下，产业端的数字化工具所承担的“补位”功能是过渡性的，还是长期可持续的，尚未有定论。

 

对于企业而言，这意味着在可预见的未来，全周期管理的商业闭环仍需要在政策缝隙中摸索。

 

据了解，BMC瑞迈特正主动将服务触角延伸至基层，深入社区开展免费呼吸慢病常识宣传与疾病筛查，将晦涩的医学术语转化为通俗易懂，同时面向呼吸慢病防治最前线的医护人员曾启动基层呼吸治疗技术培训，提升基层医务人员对呼吸慢病的识别能力及对呼吸机规范化操作的专业技能。

 

《行动意见》的发布标志着行业共识正在形成，呼吸慢病管理需要从“碎片化”走向“系统化”。产业端的探索提供了工具和路径，但全周期管理的闭环最终能否闭合，取决于支付方、服务方、使用方三端的共同成熟。当产业端的投入热情退去，这个“信息断层”还能靠谁持续填补，仍是一个开放的问题。


作者：武瑛港、崔笑语

title: Why problems with advance directives keep harming patients
summary: This is why we get it wrong As clinicians, we were taught that advance directives (ADs) and Portable Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLSTs) protect patient autonomy. So, we encourage our patien...
full_content:
This is why we get it wrong

As clinicians, we were taught that advance directives (ADs) and Portable Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLSTs) protect patient autonomy. So, we encourage our patients to complete them. Hospitals and health systems promote and measure our efforts. Public and private insurers pay for it. And policymakers celebrate them.

But these familiar tools upon which we so heavily rely at the end of life have been creating a nationwide patient safety problem. For two decades, research has consistently shown that clinicians frequently misinterpret ADs and POLSTs. This results in undertreatment. Patients who wanted life-saving treatment never received it. And misinterpretation also results in overtreatment. Patients who wished to die naturally were subjected to aggressive and painful interventions that they sought to avoid.

ADs and POLSTs are not clinically interpretable, consistently or with high quality

Physicians and clinicians make two types of interpretation errors. First, they treat patients who want resuscitation as though they are DNR just because they have an AD. Some clinicians might even convert the AD into a POLST or DNR/CMO or DNR/Limited Treatment order. Second, physicians and clinicians may treat patients with invasive procedures, intensive care, antibiotics, or prolonged treatment even though those patients carefully documented a desire for comfort-focused care. Some might even refrain from administering pain control because the POLST says “Limited Treatment” rather than “Comfort Measures Only.” Both undertreatment and overtreatment are failures of patient-centered care.

ADs are not inherently flawed. They remain valuable tools that help patients communicate their goals, reduce conflict among family members, and guide clinical decision-making. The problem is that ADs often require interpretation. That is what is broken. Interpretation is highly variable.

With ADs and POLSTs, words such as “comfort measures,” “limited treatment,” and even “do not resuscitate” mean different things to different clinicians. For example, an emergency medicine physician may interpret the document one way because the patient is a medical stranger to them, and this is a first encounter. But a palliative medicine physician may interpret the same AD/POLST differently because they have a longer relationship with the patient and understand their goals.

When ambiguity exists, patient safety suffers. We trivialize the problem by calling it “discordance.” But it is harmful medical error that should never occur.

Over several years, multiple TRIAD studies involving emergency physicians, EMS personnel, and other physician specialties have demonstrated significant discordance between what patients want and how clinicians interpreted their ADs. Perhaps the most concerning finding is that 80 percent of physicians, 88 percent of nurses, and 90 percent of EMS mistakenly equate the mere presence of an AD with an automatic DNR order. Similarly, studies reveal significant misinterpretation rates with POLST as well as discordant understanding between what clinicians document and what the patient or agent expects. Adding scientific rigor, TRIAD findings have been reproduced by independent research teams.

Think about that for a moment. That is a complete failure.

Patient safety suffers as medical errors grow

Suppose a patient completes an AD as a part of good estate planning, specifically requesting treatment in certain circumstances. Unfortunately, contrary to those instructions, many clinicians will withhold that treatment, erroneously equating the very presence of an AD with a desire to forgo treatment.

No physician would accept a medication error rate approaching these levels. We would never tolerate widespread confusion surrounding insulin dosing, anticoagulation management, or procedural safety checklists. Yet when it comes to end-of-life decision-making, we assume traditional ADs and POLSTs are sufficient.

They are not.

Wrongful prolongation of life litigation has been expanding

Traditionally, clinicians perceived little legal risk from misinterpreting ADs. After all, how could a patient be “harmed” from saving their life? But that’s been changing. Over the past decade, courts across the country have increasingly recognized claims for wrongful prolongation of life. We now have a long line of appellate judgments, jury verdicts, and settlements against clinicians and health care entities. The cases confirm that administering CPR to a patient contrary to their AD or POLST violates that patient’s rights. And it increasingly results in civil or disciplinary penalties.

Video reduces misinterpretation errors and helps assure value-congruent care

Medicine has repeatedly demonstrated that communication improves when information is delivered through multiple channels. We use imaging, laboratory data, electronic alerts, and checklists to reduce errors. Advance care planning (ACP) and end-of-life planning should be the same.

Video has an effective and important role here. We commonly utilize videos to educate patients making decisions. We use video-based patient decision aids to support informed consent and shared decision-making. But we fail to use videos to support communication in the opposite direction. We do not use patient-created videos to inform medical teams. This is called patient-to-clinician video (PCV).

A brief prescribed patient-recorded video does something a document cannot. It captures the patient’s voice, facial expressions, emotions, reasoning, and values. It allows clinicians and family members to hear directly from the individual whose wishes are at stake. Moreover, PCV is also evidence-based as shown in the TRIAD VIII multicenter nationwide study.

A physician reviewing a video is not interpreting stale words on a page. They are hearing the patient themselves explain what matters most to them.

The goal is not to replace ADs and POLSTs. The goal is to strengthen these tools and make them safer. As shown in figure 1, this is an evolutionary process. But it has not significantly adopted available technology to make this safer for patients.

Imagine a future when a clinician can immediately access (in seconds) both a patient’s written AD/POLST and a short video explanation. The document provides legal structure. The video provides context. Together, they reduce uncertainty and improve confidence for families and clinicians alike. At its core, this is a patient safety issue.

Assure accurate AD and POLST interpretation with better tools

Every day, health care organizations invest enormous resources to prevent medical errors. Yet one of the most consequential decisions in medicine, whether to provide or withhold life-sustaining treatment, still relies heavily on documents that are frequently misunderstood in both their paper and digitized forms.

Patients deserve better. Families deserve better. And physicians and clinicians deserve tools that allow them to honor patient wishes with clarity and confidence.

To truly respect patient autonomy, we must move beyond simply asking patients to complete forms or have conversations. We must ensure that those forms are understood correctly when treatment decisions must be made by a medical stranger, or when a moment of crisis arrives. Advance directives and POLSTs work only when everyone interprets them the same way.

Figure 1: Depicting the evolution of ACP tools

Ferdinando Mirarchi is the chief executive officer and chief medical officer of MIDEO Health Technologies, LLC. He is the principal investigator of the TRIAD (The Realistic Interpretation of Advance Directives) Research Series, which identified a significant patient safety risk involving the misinterpretation of living wills, DNR orders, and Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST).

His research has been featured by The New York Times, The Washington Post, and other national media outlets, and it led to the development of MIDEO (My Informed Decision on VidEO), an evidence-based video advance directive and portable physician medical order designed to clarify patient wishes and improve emergency decision-making.

He is a reviewer for leading peer-reviewed journals, including CHEST, JAMA, and JAGS, serves on the editorial board of Patient Safety magazine, and authored Understanding Your Living Will. A fellow of both the American College of Emergency Physicians and the American Academy of Emergency Medicine, he previously held multiple leadership positions at UPMC Hamot and chaired the national palliative care committee at US Acute Care Solutions.

He shares updates on LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, and X.

Thaddeus Mason Pope is an attorney.
